Chapter 2 Project description 2.1 Prepare the R environment

Chapter 2 Project description This webbook contains all the code used for data analysis in our study on the hologenomic ecology of wild possums. We integrate host genomic variation with shotgun metagenomic profiles of the gut microbiome to examine how environment and diet are associated with microbial composition, diversity, and function. We sampled free-ranging possums across multiple sites and environment types (e.g., contrasting habitat/land-use categories), recorded basic covariates (such as sex and body measurements), and generated both host and microbial DNA data from faecal material. Rather than imposing laboratory treatments, this study leverages natural ecological variation to test whether differences among environment types and related ecological factors are linked to shifts in the gut microbiome and to host genetic backgrounds. Analytically, the webbook documents the complete workflow: data import and quality control; mapping and recovery metrics; taxonomic and functional summaries; diversity analyses (Hill numbers) and community structure tests; and differential abundance comparisons across environment types and other covariates. Where relevant, we also relate microbial features (e.g., dominant taxa, MAGs, and pathway profiles) to host genomic patterns to explore potential hologenomic links between ecology, microbiota, and host variation. Together, these analyses provide a reproducible, end-to-end account of how we interrogate possum hologenomes to understand microbiome–environment–host relationships in the wild. 2.1 Prepare the R environment 2.1.1 Environment To reproduce all the analyses locally, clone this repository in your computer using: RStudio > New Project > Version Control > Git And indicating the following git repository: ##included later Once the R project has been created, follow the instructions and code chunks shown in this webbook. 2.1.2 Libraries The following R packages are required for the data analysis. # Base library(dplyr) library(forcats) library(janitor) library(purrr) library(readr) library(readxl) library(rlang) library(stringr) library(tibble) library(tidyr) library(xml2) # for tree handling library(ape) library(phytools) # for statistics library(ANCOMBC) library(Hmsc) library(Rtsne) library(broom.mixed) library(distillR) library(emmeans) library(geiger) library(hilldiv2) library(lme4) library(nlme) library(phyloseq) library(spaa) library(vegan) library(pairwiseAdonis) # map visualisation library(exactextractr) library(geodata) library(rnaturalearth) library(rnaturalearthdata) library(sf) library(terra) # other library(corrplot) library(cowplot) library(devtools) library(GGally) library(ggnewscale) library(ggplot2) library(ggpubr) library(ggrepel) library(ggh4x) library(ggtree) library(ggtreeExtra) library(gridExtra) library(knitr) library(patchwork) library(pheatmap) library(R.utils) library(RColorBrewer) library(rairtable) library(tinytable) library(UpSetR) library(ComplexUpset) # for web/API interactions library(httr) library(jsonlite)

Chapter 3 Prepare data 3.1 Load data 3.2 load_read_counts 3.3 load_genome_metadata 3.4 Genome base hits 3.5 Genome tree 3.6 Genome annotations 3.7 Filter reads by coverage 3.8 Transform reads into genome counts 3.9 Prepare color scheme 3.10 Wrap working objects

Chapter 3 Prepare data We load pipeline outputs and metadata, harmonise identifiers, and derive working objects used downstream: coverage-filtered counts, genome lengths and phylogeny, genome annotations (via Airtable), colour palettes, and GIFT-based functional tables. Everything is wrapped as a single RData for reuse. 3.1 Load data Load the original data files outputted by the bioinformatic pipeline. 3.1.1 Sample metadata Note: Load sample metadata from the merged metadata file. The first column is renamed to “sample” to ensure consistent naming across the analysis. sample_metadata <- read_tsv("data/merged_metadata.tsv") %>% rename(sample=1) 3.2 load_read_counts Note: Load read count data from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome” and select only columns corresponding to samples present in the metadata. This ensures data consistency between counts and metadata. read_counts <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_counts.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(one_of(c("genome",sample_metadata$sample))) # Select specific columns from the data 3.3 load_genome_metadata Note: Load genome metadata (MAG information) from the compressed TSV file. Rename “mag_size” to “length” for consistency. Filter to only include genomes present in the read counts data and arrange them in the same order as read_counts to ensure alignment across datasets. genome_metadata <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_mag_info.tsv.gz") %>% rename(length=mag_size)%>% semi_join(., read_counts, by = "genome") %>% arrange(match(genome,read_counts$genome)) 3.4 Genome base hits Note: Load genome coverage data (base hits) from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome”, select only columns for samples in metadata, filter to genomes present in genome_metadata, and arrange in the same order as read_counts. This coverage data is used to filter low-coverage genomes. genome_coverage <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_coverage.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(one_of(c("genome",sample_metadata$sample)))%>% # Select specific columns from the data semi_join(., genome_metadata, by = "genome")%>% arrange(match(genome, read_counts$genome)) 3.5 Genome tree Note: Load the phylogenetic tree of genomes from the compressed Newick file. Remove single quotes from tip labels (MAG names) and prune the tree to only include tips corresponding to genomes in the metadata. This ensures the tree matches the genomes used in downstream analyses. genome_tree <- read_tree("data/DMB0167.tree.gz") genome_tree$tip.label <- str_replace_all(genome_tree$tip.label,"'", "") #remove single quotes in MAG names genome_tree <- keep.tip(genome_tree, tip=genome_metadata$genome) # keep only MAG tips 3.6 Genome annotations Note: Download genome annotation files from ERDA using Airtable metadata. This chunk connects to Airtable, retrieves annotation URLs for MAGs with genes, downloads all annotation tables, and combines them into a single compressed file. This only needs to be run once to generate the genome_annotations table. Note that the Airtable connection requires a personal access token. airtable("MAGs", "appWbHBNLE6iAsMRV") %>% #get base ID from Airtable browser URL read_airtable(., fields = c("ID","mag_name","number_genes","anno_url"), id_to_col = TRUE) %>% #get 3 columns from MAGs table filter(mag_name %in% paste0(genome_metadata$genome,".fa")) %>% #filter by MAG name filter(number_genes > 0) %>% #genes need to exist select(anno_url) %>% #list MAG annotation urls pull() %>% read_tsv() %>% #load all tables rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) %>% #rename first 3 columns write_tsv(file="data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz") #write to overall compressed file Note: Load the pre-generated genome annotations table from the compressed file. Rename the first three columns to “gene”, “genome”, and “contig” for consistency. This annotation data is used for functional analysis using the GIFT framework. genome_annotations <- read_tsv("data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz") %>% rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) 3.7 Filter reads by coverage Note: Filter read counts based on genome coverage. Set minimum coverage threshold (0.3) and create a binary mask where genomes with coverage above the threshold are kept (1) and below are excluded (0). Multiply read counts by this mask to zero out reads from low-coverage genomes, ensuring only high-quality genome assignments are retained. min_coverage=0.3 read_counts_filt <- genome_coverage %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(. > min_coverage, 1, 0))) %>% # Add or modify columns in the dataset mutate(across(-1, ~ . * read_counts[[cur_column()]])) # Add or modify columns in the dataset 3.8 Transform reads into genome counts Note: Transform raw read counts into normalized genome counts by dividing by genome length (scaled by read length). This accounts for the fact that longer genomes will naturally have more reads mapped to them, normalizing counts to represent relative abundance rather than absolute read numbers. readlength=150 genome_counts <- read_counts %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . / (genome_metadata$length / readlength) )) # Add or modify columns in the dataset Note: Transform filtered read counts (after coverage filtering) into normalized genome counts using the same length normalization approach. This creates the filtered genome count matrix used in downstream analyses, excluding low-coverage genomes. readlength=150 genome_counts_filt <- read_counts_filt %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . / (genome_metadata$length / readlength) )) # Add or modify columns in the dataset 3.8.1 Distill annotations into GIFTs Note: Convert genome annotations into GIFT (Genome-Inferred Functional Traits) format using the distillR package. This aggregates gene-level annotations into functional trait profiles for each genome, which are used for community-level functional analysis. The function processes annotations from columns 9, 10, and 19 of the annotation table. genome_gifts <- distill(genome_annotations,GIFT_db2,genomecol=2,annotcol=c(9,10,19), verbosity=F) 3.9 Prepare color scheme Note: Load phylum-level color scheme from the EHI taxonomy color repository. Join with genome metadata to get colors for phyla present in the dataset, arrange to match the tree tip order, and create a named vector mapping phylum names to colors. This ensures consistent color coding across all visualizations. phylum_colors <- read_tsv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earthhologenome/EHI_taxonomy_colour/main/ehi_phylum_colors.tsv") %>% right_join(genome_metadata, by=join_by(phylum == phylum)) %>% arrange(match(genome, genome_tree$tip.label)) %>% select(phylum, colors) %>% unique() %>% arrange(phylum) %>% pull(colors, name=phylum) Note: Classify samples into geographic regions (Tasmania vs Australia) based on latitude and longitude coordinates. Samples within the specified geographic bounds are classified as “Tasmania”, all others as “Australia”. This creates a categorical variable for geographic analysis. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% mutate( island = case_when( latitude < -38 & latitude > -45 & longitude > 140 & longitude < 150 ~ "Tasmania", TRUE ~ "Australia" ) ) 3.10 Wrap working objects Note: Save all processed data objects into a single RData file for efficient loading in downstream analyses. This includes sample metadata, genome metadata, read counts, normalized genome counts (both filtered and unfiltered), phylogenetic tree, GIFT functional annotations, and color schemes. All subsequent chapters load this single file to access the prepared data. save(sample_metadata, genome_metadata, read_counts, genome_counts, genome_counts_filt, genome_tree, genome_gifts, phylum_colors, file = "data/data.Rdata")

Chapter 4 Data statistics Note: Load all required data objects including sample metadata, genome counts, and other prepared datasets from the RData file created in the data preparation chapter. load("data/data.Rdata") #Visualisation of geographical location of samples and their respectiv envirotypes 4.1 Helper Functions Note: Define helper function to filter and aggregate geographic data by environment variable. This eliminates code duplication and allows reuse for both broad and local environment classifications. 4.2 Filter Data Note: Filter sample metadata by geographic boundaries to create datasets for full Australia/Tasmania region and Tasmania-only region. Aggregate sample counts per location and broad environment type to prepare data for mapping visualization. # Filter by broad environment broad_env_data <- filter_geographic_data(sample_metadata, "broad_environment") full_possums <- broad_env_data$full_possums tasmania_possums <- broad_env_data$tasmania_possums full_possums_count <- broad_env_data$full_possums_count tasmania_possums_count <- broad_env_data$tasmania_possums_count 4.3 Load Map Note: Load Australia country boundary data from Natural Earth dataset to use as the base map for geographic visualizations. This provides the geographic context for plotting sample locations. # Load world map australia_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>% filter(admin == "Australia") 4.4 Plot Possum Locations Note: Create two side-by-side map visualizations showing sample locations colored by broad environment type. The first plot shows the full dataset across Australia, while the second plot zooms into Tasmania. Point sizes represent the number of samples per location. Combine both plots and save to PDF for publication. # Count total possums total_full <- sum(full_possums_count$count) total_tasmania <- sum(tasmania_possums_count$count) # Plot 1: Full Dataset (Including Border Data) map_plot_full <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + # Base map geom_point(data = full_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = broad_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Full Dataset (", total_full, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Environment Type", size = "Count") + theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")) # Plot 2: Zoomed-in Tasmania (with entire landmass and cleaned longitude labels) map_plot_zoomed <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + # Base map geom_point(data = tasmania_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = broad_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + coord_sf(xlim = c(143, 149), ylim = c(-44, -39)) + # Full Tasmania view theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Tasmania (", total_tasmania, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Environment Type", size = "Count") + theme(legend.position = "right", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5), plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")) combined_plot <- (map_plot_full + map_plot_zoomed) + plot_layout(guides = "collect", widths = c(1, 1.2)) combined_plot # ---- SAVE TO PDF ---- ggsave( filename = "Sample _maps.pdf", plot = combined_plot, width = 8, # adjust for your needs height = 4, # adjust for your needs units = "in", device = cairo_pdf # nice for text/embedding fonts ) Note: Filter sample metadata again, this time grouping by local_environment instead of broad_environment. This creates alternative datasets for mapping with more detailed environment classifications. Aggregate sample counts per location and local environment type. # Filter by local environment local_env_data <- filter_geographic_data(sample_metadata, "local_environment") full_possums <- local_env_data$full_possums tasmania_possums <- local_env_data$tasmania_possums full_possums_count <- local_env_data$full_possums_count tasmania_possums_count <- local_env_data$tasmania_possums_count 4.5 Plot Possum Locations Note: Create two side-by-side map visualizations showing sample locations colored by local environment type using a viridis color scale. The first plot shows the full dataset, while the second plot zooms into Tasmania. This provides a more detailed view of environmental classifications compared to the broad environment maps. # Count total possums total_full <- sum(full_possums_count$count) total_tasmania <- sum(tasmania_possums_count$count) # Plot 1: Full Dataset (Including Border Data) map_plot_full <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + geom_point(data = full_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = local_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Full Dataset (", total_full, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"), legend.position = "none" ) # Plot 2: Zoomed-in Tasmania map_plot_zoomed <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + geom_point(data = tasmania_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = local_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + coord_sf(xlim = c(143, 149), ylim = c(-44, -39)) + scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Tasmania (", total_tasmania, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "none" ) # Combine the plots side by side (map_plot_full + map_plot_zoomed) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2)) Note: Create a custom legend plot showing all local environment types with their average sample counts. This standalone legend can be used alongside the maps to clearly identify environment types and their relative sampling intensity. The legend is ordered by mean count and uses the same color scheme as the maps. # Step 1: Create simplified/aggregated legend data legend_data <- tasmania_possums_count %>% group_by(local_environment) %>% summarise(mean_count = mean(count, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% filter(!is.na(local_environment)) %>% arrange(desc(mean_count)) %>% mutate(env_label = local_environment) # Step 2: Plot custom "legend" with clean layout custom_legend_plot <- ggplot(legend_data, aes(x = 1, y = reorder(env_label, mean_count), color = env_label, size = mean_count)) + geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 6)) + # tweak dot size scaling scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + theme( axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(10, 30, 10, 10), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 0) ) # Show it custom_legend_plot 4.6 Sequencing reads statistics Note: Calculate summary statistics for sequencing reads across all samples. Convert read counts to gigabases (GB) by multiplying by read length (150 bp) and dividing by 1 billion. Compute total, mean, and standard deviation, then format as “mean ± SD” for display in a formatted table. sample_metadata %>% summarise(Total=sum(reads_post_fastp * 150 / 1000000000) %>% round(2), mean=mean(reads_post_fastp * 150 / 1000000000) %>% round(2), sd=sd(reads_post_fastp * 150 / 1000000000) %>% round(2)) %>% unite("Average",mean, sd, sep = " ± ", remove = TRUE) %>% tt() .table td.tinytable_css_fraontgcko4vc3bhfrfv, .table th.tinytable_css_fraontgcko4vc3bhfrfv { border-top: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.05em; } .table td.tinytable_css_5ne4b5o2dd63f27c3aly, .table th.tinytable_css_5ne4b5o2dd63f27c3aly { border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; } Total Average 354.78 4.86 ± 1.43 4.7 DNA fractions Note: Calculate the distribution of sequencing data across different categories: low quality bases (removed during quality filtering), bases mapped to host genome, unmapped bases (microbial but not in MAGs), and bases mapped to MAGs. Compute these fractions for each sample and convert to gigabases. Display per-sample breakdown and overall mean values in formatted tables. sequence_fractions <- read_counts %>% pivot_longer(-genome, names_to = "sample", values_to = "value") %>% group_by(sample) %>% Add statistics for each group value if provided if (!is.null(group_col) && !is.null(group_values)) { for (val in group_values) { group_stats <- data %>% filter(.data[[group_col]] == val) %>% group_by(across(all_of(tax_col))) %>% summarise( mean_val = mean(relabun * 100, na.rm = TRUE), sd_val = sd(relabun * 100, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) result <- result %>% left_join(group_stats, by = tax_col) %>% rename(!!str_c(val, "_mean") := mean_val, !!str_c(val, "_sd") := sd_val) } } # Chapter 7 Alpha diversity 7.1 microbiota

Chapter 7 Alpha diversity We quantify within-sample diversity using Hill numbers: richness (q0), neutral/abundance-weighted (q1), phylogenetic (q1 + tree), and functional (q1 + traits), and compare these across environments and sex. 7.1 microbiota Note: Load all required data objects including genome counts, metadata, and color schemes. Set factor levels for broad_environment variable to ensure consistent ordering. load("data/data.Rdata") treatment_colors <- c("#f56042","#429ef5", "#42f58d", "#b142f5", "#FFA500") sample_metadata$broad_environment <- factor(sample_metadata$broad_environment, levels=c("1000198 - Mixed forest", "1000221 - Temperate woodland", "1000218 - Xeric shrubland", "1000215 - Temperate shrubland", "1000245 - Cropland")) Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 and filter genome counts to only include valid samples. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") valid_samples <- sample_metadata$sample genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% dplyr::select(genome, tidyselect::any_of(valid_samples)) Note: Prune the phylogenetic tree to match genomes present in the filtered count data. Identifies genomes that exist in both the count data and the tree, then removes tree tips that don’t have corresponding count data. # 1) Figure out the common labels otus <- genome_counts_filt$genome tips <- genome_tree$tip.label common <- intersect(tips, otus) # 2) Prune the tree to only those tips genome_tree_pruned <- drop.tip(genome_tree, setdiff(tips, common)) 7.1.1 Hill numbers Richness of microbiotic species in samples Note: Calculate four types of Hill number diversity metrics for each sample: richness (q=0, species count unweighted by abundance), neutral (q=1, Shannon diversity abundance-weighted), phylogenetic (q=1 + tree, incorporates phylogenetic relationships), and functional (q=1 + traits, incorporates functional trait distances). Then merge all metrics into a single alpha_div dataframe. # Calculate Hill numbers richness <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 0) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(richness = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") neutral <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(neutral = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") phylogenetic <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1, tree = genome_tree_pruned) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(phylogenetic = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") # Aggregate basal GIFT into elements dist <- genome_gifts %>% to.elements(., GIFT_db) %>% traits2dist(., method = "gower") functional <- genome_counts_filt %>% filter(genome %in% rownames(dist)) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1, dist = dist) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(functional = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") %>% mutate(functional = if_else(is.nan(functional), 1, functional)) # Merge all metrics alpha_div <- richness %>% full_join(neutral, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% full_join(phylogenetic, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% full_join(functional, by = join_by(sample == sample)) Note: Create a summary statistics table showing mean ± SD for each alpha diversity metric. Chapter 12 environmental permanova We test whether environmental α-diversity (Hill h0/h1/h2 of land-cover) relates to microbiome β-diversity (Bray–Curtis), and visualise relationships (e.g., NMDS axes vs. Hill metrics) and distance-matrix structure. 12.1 Load data Note: Load all required data objects including sample metadata, beta diversity matrices, and Hill diversity metrics from the RData files created in previous chapters. 12.2 Data preparation Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 from the metadata and Hill diversity data. This sample was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") hill_long <- hill_long %>% dplyr::filter(id != "EHI01340") Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Join with sample metadata to create a combined metadata object for downstream analyses. 12.3 Helper functions Note: Helper function to align metadata with distance matrices. This eliminates code duplication when aligning metadata for multiple distance matrices. Defined early as it’s needed by multiple analysis sections. Note: Optimized helper function that accepts pre-calculated NMDS object instead of recalculating. This eliminates redundant NMDS calculations when creating multiple plots. 12.4 Ordination analysis Note: Extract distance matrices from beta diversity objects for use in ordination analyses. These matrices represent Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between samples at different diversity orders. Note: Calculate all NMDS ordinations once upfront. These are expensive operations (trymax = 500 iterations each) and were previously calculated redundantly 3+ times. This optimization saves significant computation time. Note: Align metadata with each distance matrix using the helper function. This ensures proper sample order matching for ordination and visualization. 12.5 Grouping variables Note: Create grouping variables for environmental Hill diversity metrics. Calculate medians once to avoid redundant calculations. Split into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) and median-based groups (Low, High) for visualization and statistical testing. Note: Verify the grouping variables were created correctly by displaying frequency tables. This ensures balanced group sizes for downstream analyses. 12.10 Visualization Associations between environmental α-diversity (Hill h0/h1/h2) and microbiome ordination (NMDS1/2), with fitted vectors and a subset heatmap of Bray–Curtis distances. Note: Create combined scatterplots showing relationships between all environmental Hill diversity metrics and NMDS ordination axes. This provides a comprehensive view of how environmental diversity relates to microbiome β-diversity ordination. Uses loess smoothing instead of linear regression, which is more appropriate for potentially non-linear relationships. Note: Fit environmental Hill diversity vectors (h0, h1, h2) onto the q0 NMDS ordination using envfit. This tests the correlation between environmental variables and ordination axes, displaying significant vectors as arrows on the ordination plot. Improved visualization using ggplot2 for consistency with other plots. Note: Create an improved heatmap visualization of Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix with sample grouping information. This shows clustering patterns in microbiome β-diversity and how they relate to environmental Hill diversity groups. Uses all samples (or a representative subset if too large) with grouping annotations. #abundance analysis of micrb community in diffrent enviroment diversitys This chapter analyzes differential abundance of microbial genomes between samples with low and high environmental diversity (Hill diversity metrics h0, h1, h2). We use ANCOM-BC2 to identify significantly differentially abundant genomes and visualize results with barplots and volcano plots. 12.11 Load data Note: Load sample metadata, genome count data, and Hill diversity metrics from RData files created in previous chapters. Filter out sample EHI01340 which was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Join with sample metadata to create a combined metadata object for downstream analyses. 12.12 Data preparation Note: Create grouping variables for each Hill diversity metric (q0, q1, q2). Split samples into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) based on environmental Hill diversity, then filter to keep only Low and High groups for two-group comparisons. For each q value, create filtered metadata and genome count matrices containing only samples in Low/High groups and genomes present in at least one sample. n filtered_inputs = 3 q=0 nLow=30 nHigh=20 genomes=1750 q=1 nLow=25 nHigh=17 genomes=1522 q=2 nLow=24 nHigh=17 genomes=1514 12.13 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. This is important for ANCOM-BC2 analysis as structural zeros can be handled explicitly. For each q value, calculate which genomes are structurally absent in Low vs High groups and compute group means for genomes that are present in only one group. Note: Create UpSet plot using UpSetR to visualize the intersection of genomes present in Low and High environmental diversity groups. The plot shows unique genomes in each group and shared genomes, with colors indicating group membership. 12.14 Differential abundance analysis 12.14.1 Build phyloseq objects Note: Create phyloseq objects for each q value (q0, q1, q2) containing OTU table (genome counts), taxonomy table, and sample metadata. Counts are kept as integers with zeros allowed, as ANCOM-BC2 can handle zeros without requiring pseudocounts. Sample metadata includes the grouping variable (Low/High) for each Hill diversity metric. 12.14.2 Run ANCOM-BC2 analysis Note: Perform ANCOM-BC2 differential abundance testing for each q value, comparing Low vs High environmental diversity groups. The analysis uses structural zero modeling (struc_zero=TRUE) to properly handle genomes absent in one group. Version-adaptive code handles differences between ANCOMBC package versions. Results include log fold-changes, p-values, and adjusted p-values for each genome. 12.14.3 Visualize differential abundance results Note: Extract significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05) from ANCOM-BC2 results and create visualizations. Barplots show log2 fold-changes for significant genomes, ordered by effect size and colored by phylum. Volcano plots show all tested genomes with log2 fold-change on x-axis and -log10(p-value) on y-axis, highlighting significant hits. Both visualizations are created for each q value (q0, q1, q2). Note: Alternative barplot visualization using genome identifiers instead of taxon names. This provides a different view of the same differential abundance results, useful for identifying specific genomes of interest. 12.15 Alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros Note: Run an alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with additional structural zero handling parameters. This analysis uses a random effects model (rand_formula=“~1”) and different parameter settings including Holm p-value adjustment, pseudo-sensitivity analysis, and explicit structural zero detection. This provides a complementary view to the main analysis and may identify additional differentially abundant genomes. Note: Extract and clean results from the alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros. Filter for significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05), join with taxonomy information, and create cleaned tables ready for visualization or further analysis. Results are organized by log fold-change for easy interpretation. 12.16 Load data Note: Load sample metadata, genome count data, and Hill diversity metrics from RData files created in previous chapters. These data objects will be used for diversity and abundance analysis comparing samples with low and high environmental diversity. 12.17 Data preparation Note: Exclude outlier sample EHI01340 from all datasets. Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format and join with sample metadata. Choose a Hill diversity metric (default: h1, exponential Shannon) to split samples into tertiles. Filter to keep only Low and High groups (excluding Mid) for two-group comparisons. Ensure sample metadata and genome count matrices are aligned, keeping only samples present in both datasets and genomes with at least one non-zero count. # --- Configuration: outlier sample to exclude ------------------------------ outlier_sample <- "EHI01340" # Check if outlier sample exists (may already be excluded in previous chapters) if (!outlier_sample %in% sample_metadata$sample) { message("Note: Outlier sample '", outlier_sample, "' not found in sample_metadata (likely already excluded in previous chapters).") } # drop the outlier sample everywhere (safe even if already excluded) sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% filter(sample != outlier_sample) # Optimized: Filter genome counts in one pass - select valid samples and filter zero rows valid_sample_cols <- intersect(sample_metadata$sample, colnames(genome_counts_filt)) genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(valid_sample_cols)) %>% filter(rowSums(across(-genome, ~ .x != 0), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) # Validate filtering results if (nrow(sample_metadata) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after filtering. Check sample_metadata.") } if (nrow(genome_counts_filt) == 0) { stop("Error: No genomes remaining after filtering. Check genome_counts_filt.") } # --- choose which Hill order to split on ---------------------------------- # use "h1" by default (exp-Shannon). Change to "h0" or "h2" if you prefer. q_choice <- "h1" # Validate q_choice format valid_q_choices <- c("h0", "h1", "h2") if (!q_choice %in% valid_q_choices) { stop("Error: q_choice must be one of: ", paste(valid_q_choices, collapse = ", ")) } # Validate hill_long exists and has data if (!exists("hill_long") || nrow(hill_long) == 0) { stop("Error: hill_long is missing or empty.") } # Optimized: Build Hill-wide and join with metadata in one pipeline hill_col <- paste0("env_hill_", q_choice) hill_wide <- hill_long %>% filter(id != outlier_sample) %>% rename(sample = id) %>% pivot_wider(id_cols = sample, names_from = q, values_from = value, names_glue = "env_hill_{q}") # Validate pivot_wider results if (!hill_col %in% colnames(hill_wide)) { stop("Error: Hill diversity column '", hill_col, "' not found after pivot_wider. ", "Available columns: ", paste(colnames(hill_wide), collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Join and filter missing Hill data in one step meta_hill <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(hill_wide, by = "sample") %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[hill_col]])) # Remove samples with missing Hill diversity data # Report if any samples were excluded n_excluded_hill <- nrow(sample_metadata) - nrow(meta_hill) if (n_excluded_hill > 0) { warning("Found ", n_excluded_hill, " samples with missing Hill diversity data. These were excluded.") } # Validate we have enough samples for tertiles (need at least 3) if (nrow(meta_hill) < 3) { stop("Error: Insufficient samples (", nrow(meta_hill), ") for creating tertiles. Need at least 3 samples.") } group_col <- paste0("env_group_q", substr(q_choice, 2, 2)) # env_group_q1, etc. # tertiles → keep only Low/High (drop Mid) and fix factor order Low < High # Use tryCatch to handle edge cases in cut_number meta_hill <- tryCatch({ meta_hill %>% mutate( !!group_col := ggplot2::cut_number(.data[[hill_col]], 3, labels = c("Low","Mid","High")) ) %>% filter(.data[[group_col]] %in% c("Low","High")) %>% mutate(!!group_col := factor(.data[[group_col]], levels = c("Low","High"))) }, error = function(e) { stop("Error creating tertiles with cut_number: ", e$message, ". This may occur if there are too few unique values in ", hill_col) }) # Validate group creation if (nrow(meta_hill) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after filtering to Low/High groups.") } # Validate group creation group_counts <- table(meta_hill[[group_col]], useNA = "no") if (any(group_counts == 0)) { stop("Error: One or both groups (Low/High) are empty after filtering. ", paste(names(group_counts), group_counts, sep = "=", collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Keep only samples present in both datasets in one pass valid_samples <- intersect(meta_hill$sample, colnames(genome_counts_filt)) if (length(valid_samples) == 0) { stop("Error: No overlapping samples between meta_hill and genome_counts_filt.") } # Filter both datasets to valid samples meta_hill <- meta_hill %>% filter(sample %in% valid_samples) genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(valid_samples)) %>% # Re-filter genomes to ensure they're still present after sample filtering filter(rowSums(across(-genome, ~ .x != 0), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) # Final validation if (nrow(meta_hill) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after final filtering.") } cat("N Low / High = ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "Low"), " / ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "High"), "\n", sep = "") ## N Low / High = 25 / 17 12.18 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. Validate that the phylogenetic tree exists and prune it to match genomes present in the filtered count data. Calculate richness (q=0, species count), neutral diversity (q=1, Shannon diversity), and phylogenetic diversity (q=1 with tree) for each sample. These functions eliminate code duplication and ensure consistent extraction patterns across all analyses. # Safe correlation function that checks dimensions safe_cor <- function(x, y, ...) { if (length(x) != length(y)) { warning(paste("Vectors have incompatible dimensions:", length(x), "vs", length(y), ". Returning NA.")) return(NA) } if (length(x) == 0) { return(NA) } tryCatch({ cor(x, y, ...) }, error = function(e) { warning(paste("Error computing correlation:", e$message)) return(NA) }) } # Extract beta mean estimate for a specific covariate get_beta_estimate <- function(fit_model_14, model_obj, covariate_name) { getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_14, parName = "Beta")$mean %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable = model_obj$covNames) %>% filter(variable == covariate_name) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "mean") %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean) } # Extract beta support values for a specific covariate get_beta_support <- function(fit_model_14, model_obj, covariate_name) { getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_14, parName = "Beta")$support %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable = model_obj$covNames) %>% filter(variable == covariate_name) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "support") %>% dplyr::select(genome, support) } # Extract beta credible intervals for a specific covariate get_beta_ci <- function(fit_model_14, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9)) { beta_q <- getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_14, parName = "Beta", q = quantiles)$q idx_cov <- which(model_obj$covNames == covariate_name) n_genomes <- length(model_obj$spNames) purrr::map_dfr(1:n_genomes, ~ { tibble( genome = model_obj$spNames[.x], q10 = beta_q[1, idx_cov, .x], q90 = beta_q[2, idx_cov, .x] ) }) } # Combine beta estimate, support, and credible intervals with metadata get_beta_complete <- function(fit_model_14, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9)) { estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_14, model_obj, covariate_name) ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_14, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles) ci %>% right_join(estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") } # Calculate functional differences between positive and negative associations calculate_functional_differences <- function(elements_response, variable_name) { var_sym <- rlang::sym(variable_name) elements_response %>% filter(!!var_sym != "Neutral") %>% mutate(!!var_sym := droplevels(!!var_sym)) %>% group_by(GIFT) %>% summarise( n_pos = sum(!!var_sym == "Positive"), n_neg = sum(!!var_sym == "Negative"), mean_pos = mean(value[!!var_sym == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_neg = mean(value[!!var_sym == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE), diff = mean_pos - mean_neg, p = if (n_pos > 1 && n_neg > 1 && stats::sd(value[!!var_sym == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0 && stats::sd(value[!!var_sym == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0) { stats::t.test(value ~ !!var_sym, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value } else NA_real_, .groups = "drop" ) %>% mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")) %>% arrange(p_adj) } # Create volcano plot for functional differences create_volcano_plot <- function(functional_differences, variable_label, gift_colors) { fc_threshold <- 0.2 fdr_threshold <- 0.05 plot_data <- functional_differences %>% mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% mutate( p_adj_plot = ifelse(is.na(p_adj) | p_adj == 0, .Machine$double.xmin, p_adj), neglog10_fdr = -log10(p_adj_plot), hit = !is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < fdr_threshold & abs(diff) >= fc_threshold ) %>% mutate(func = ifelse(hit, func, "NS")) %>% filter(neglog10_fdr < 20) # Build color palette func_levels <- sort(unique(plot_data$func)) palette_df <- tibble(func = func_levels) %>% left_join( gift_colors %>% select(func = Code_function, Color), by = "func" ) %>% mutate( Color = case_when( func == "NS" & is.na(Color) ~ "grey70", is.na(Color) ~ "#999999", TRUE ~ Color ) ) color_values <- setNames(palette_df$Color, palette_df$func) plot_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = neglog10_fdr, color = func)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-fc_threshold, fc_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0, 15) + xlim(-0.6, 0.6) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = subset(plot_data, hit), aes(label = GIFT), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0 ) + scale_color_manual(values = color_values) + labs( x = "Mean difference (Positive − Negative)", y = expression(-log[10]("FDR (BH)")), color = "Group", subtitle = paste0("Thresholds: |diff| ≥ ", fc_threshold, ", FDR < ", fdr_threshold) ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) } # Aggregate beta coefficients by taxonomic level aggregate_by_taxonomy <- function(ci_data, tax_level = "phylum") { tax_sym <- rlang::sym(tax_level) ci_data %>% group_by(!!tax_sym) %>% summarise( mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10 = stats::quantile(mean, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE), q90 = stats::quantile(mean, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) } # Aggregate beta coefficients by functional group aggregate_by_function <- function(ci_data, elements_response, gift_colors, n_top = 15, min_genomes = 3) { # Extract genome effects genome_effects <- ci_data %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean, q10, q90) # Map genomes to functional groups genome_func <- elements_response %>% dplyr::filter(value > 0) %>% dplyr::mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% dplyr::distinct(genome, func) # Summarise by functional group func_summary <- genome_func %>% dplyr::left_join(genome_effects, by = "genome") %>% dplyr::group_by(func) %>% dplyr::summarise( n_genomes = sum(!is.na(mean)), mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), q90_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) %>% dplyr::filter(n_genomes >= min_genomes) # Add labels and colors func_top %>% dplyr::left_join( gift_colors %>% dplyr::transmute( func = Code_function, func_label = legend, color = Color ), by = "func" ) %>% dplyr::mutate( func_label = ifelse(is.na(func_label), func, func_label) ) } # Create a scatter plot showing beta coefficient (x-axis) versus posterior probability (y-axis), colored by phylum for genomes with significant associations. This visualization helps identify genomes with strong and well-supported devil associations. # Extract beta estimate and support using helper functions devil_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_14, m, "devil") devil_support <- get_beta_support(fit_model_14, m, "devil") devil_beta <- inner_join(devil_estimate, devil_support, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") # Optional: precompute x-limits if you really want them devil_xrange <- range(devil_beta$mean, na.rm = TRUE) devil_xlim <- devil_xrange + c(-0.05, 0.05) devil_beta %>% mutate( significant = support >= support_threshold | support <= negsupport_threshold, support_plot = ifelse(mean < 0, 1 - support, support), # support for the sign of beta phylum_sig = ifelse(significant & support_plot > 0.9, phylum, NA) ) %>% ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = support_plot, colour = phylum_sig)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) + scale_color_manual(values = phylum_colors, na.translate = FALSE) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + # if you want the x-limits, now this is safe: xlim(devil_xlim) + labs( x = "Devil β coefficient", y = "Posterior probability (|β| > 0)", colour = "Phylum" ) + theme_minimal() ## Devil credible intervals Note: Calculate 10% and 90% credible intervals for devil beta coefficients. Filter to genomes with credible non-zero effects (where the credible interval does not include zero) and create a forest plot showing beta estimates with error bars, ordered by effect size. # Credible intervals for 'devil' using helper function devil_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_14, m, "devil") devil_ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_14, m, "devil") %>% right_join(devil_estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") # Genomes with credible non-zero devil effect devil_ci %>% filter(q10 > 0 | q90 < 0) %>% create_forest_plot( color_var = "phylum", color_values = phylum_colors, x_lab = "Devil β coefficient", y_lab = "Genomes", show_legend = FALSE ) ## Devil top genomes Note: Identify the top 30 genomes with the strongest positive and top 30 with the strongest negative devil associations (based on credible intervals). Create a focused forest plot showing only these top genomes with their credible intervals, providing a clear view of the most extreme devil associations. # Reuse devil_ci from previous chunk if available, otherwise create it if (!exists("devil_ci")) { devil_estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_14, m, "devil") devil_ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_14, m, "devil") %>% right_join(devil_estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") } # Keep only genomes with credible non-zero effect devil_ci_sig <- devil_ci %>% filter(q10 > 0 | q90 < 0) # 4. Take top N positive and top N negative genomes N_top <- 30 devil_ci_top <- devil_ci_sig %>% slice_max(order_by = mean, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) %>% bind_rows( devil_ci_sig %>% slice_min(order_by = mean, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) ) %>% distinct(genome, .keep_all = TRUE) # 5. Chapter 15 Hmsc analysis Note: Load all required data objects including genome counts, metadata, GIFT database, and color schemes. Read GIFT color mapping file to create legend labels for functional groups. load("data/data.Rdata") gift_colors <- read_tsv("data/gift_colors.tsv") %>% mutate(legend=str_c(Code_function," - ",Function)) ## Rows: 21 Columns: 3 ## ── Column specification ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ## Delimiter: "\t" ## chr (3): Code_function, Function, Color ## ## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. Note: Set HMSC model parameters for MCMC sampling: number of samples, thinning interval, transient (burn-in) period, and posterior support thresholds for determining significant associations. #Parameters nSamples=250 thin=1000 transient=nSamples * thin support_threshold=0.9 negsupport_threshold=1-support_threshold Note: Load the unfitted HMSC model object and import the fitted model posterior samples from HPC. The fitted model is downloaded from a remote server, then posterior samples are imported and processed according to the specified sampling parameters. #Load unfitted load(file = "hmsc/model_env_ani") #Load fitted (as a temporary file) tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") options(timeout = max(600, getOption("timeout"))) download.file("https://sid.erda.dk/share_redirect/Gh0WbM42c4/Hmsc_model_env_ani.rds", tmp, mode = "wb") importFromHPC = readRDS(tmp)[[1]] unlink(tmp) postList = importFromHPC[1:4] fit_model_16 = importPosteriorFromHPC(m, postList, nSamples, thin, transient) Note: Compute variance partitioning to quantify the proportion of variance explained by each environmental variable and random effect (animal, site) for each genome. Calculate predicted values and evaluate model fit using R², displaying the distribution of R² values across genomes. # Compute variance partitioning varpart=computeVariancePartitioning(fit_model_16) varpart$vals %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column(var="variable") %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(variable=factor(variable)) %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(mean=mean(value)*100,sd=sd(value)*100) %>% tt() .table td.tinytable_css_fsvv4um6wxtbb6ls7qil, .table th.tinytable_css_fsvv4um6wxtbb6ls7qil { border-top: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.05em; } .table td.tinytable_css_al07vhifv3twpcexckvn, .table th.tinytable_css_al07vhifv3twpcexckvn { border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; } variable mean sd density 4.4521451 3.7862996 development 2.6633417 1.9906652 devil 2.1603302 2.1055054 diversity 2.4635272 2.3605516 logseqdepth 6.9467598 4.7664193 precipitation 5.5090724 4.9044390 Random: animal 49.2241965 16.2548368 Random: site 19.7924978 13.8819778 sex 0.9729754 0.8693063 temperature 2.5660841 2.6909419 weight 3.2490698 2.5720832 preds = computePredictedValues(fit_model_16) MF = evaluateModelFit(hM=fit_model_16, predY=preds) hist(MF$R2, xlim = c(0,1), main=paste0("Mean = ", round(mean(MF$R2),2))) Note: Create a phylogenetic tree visualization with variance partitioning results displayed as stacked bars next to each tip. The tree shows phylum annotations and variance contributions from each predictor variable, allowing visualization of how environmental and random effects vary across the phylogenetic tree. # 1) Build the phylogeny in the same species set/order as varpart vp_tree_phylo <- genome_tree %>% keep.tip(tip = colnames(varpart$vals)) %>% force.ultrametric(method = "extend") vp_tree <- ggtree(vp_tree_phylo, size = 0.3) # 2) Phylum annotation in tree tip order phylums_vp <- genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% vp_tree$data$label) %>% arrange(match(genome, vp_tree$data$label)) %>% mutate(phylum = factor(phylum, levels = unique(phylum))) %>% column_to_rownames("genome") %>% select(phylum) vp_tree <- gheatmap( vp_tree, phylums_vp, offset = -0.2, width = 0.1, colnames = FALSE ) + scale_fill_manual(values = phylum_colors) + labs(fill = "Phylum") # start a new fill scale for the variance bars vp_tree <- vp_tree + new_scale_fill() # 3) Long variance-partitioning table varpart_long <- varpart$vals %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("variable") %>% pivot_longer( cols = -variable, names_to = "label", # must be 'label' to match tree tip labels values_to = "value" ) %>% mutate( # reorder predictors in a sensible way for the legend variable = factor( variable, levels = rev(c( "devil", "temperature", "density", "development", "weight", "precipitation", "diversity", "logseqdepth", "Random: animal", "Random: site" )) ) ) # 4) Add stacked bars with geom_fruit vp_tree + geom_fruit( data = varpart_long, geom = geom_bar, mapping = aes( x = value, y = label, fill = variable ), stat = "identity", orientation = "y", pwidth = 2, offset = 0.05 ) + labs(fill = "Variable") 15.1 Phylogenetic signal Note: Assess phylogenetic signal in the model by extracting the Rho parameter from the posterior distribution. Rho quantifies the strength of phylogenetic correlation in species responses, with values near 1 indicating strong phylogenetic signal and values near 0 indicating weak signal. Calculate credible intervals and visualize the posterior distribution. # Convert to coda object to inspect Rho (phylogenetic signal) mpost <- convertToCodaObject(fit_model_16) # Overall Rho posterior (phylogenetic signal on the species random effect) rho_vec <- unlist(mpost$Rho) # 90% credible interval and median rho_summary <- quantile(rho_vec, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) rho_summary # Optional: density plot for the appendix plot(density(rho_vec), main = "Posterior of phylogenetic signal (Rho)", xlab = "Rho") abline(v = rho_summary[2], col = "red", lty = 2) Note: Extract posterior support values for all predictor variables and create a heatmap visualization on a phylogenetic tree. The heatmap shows whether each genome has a positive, negative, or neutral association with each environmental variable based on posterior support thresholds. Phylum annotations are displayed alongside the tree tips. hmsc_tree <- genome_tree %>% keep.tip(., tip=m$spNames) # Posterior estimates post_estimates <- getPostEstimate(hM=fit_model_16, parName="Beta")$support %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable=m$covNames) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(trend = case_when( value >= support_threshold ~ "Positive", value <= negsupport_threshold ~ "Negative", TRUE ~ "Neutral")) post_table <- post_estimates %>% mutate(genome=factor(genome, levels=rev(hmsc_tree$tip.label))) %>% select(-trend) %>% mutate(value = case_when( value >= support_threshold ~ "Positive", value <= negsupport_threshold ~ "Negative", TRUE ~ "Neutral")) %>% mutate(value=factor(value, levels=c("Positive","Neutral","Negative"))) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value) %>% rename(intercept=2) %>% column_to_rownames(var="genome") %>% select(-intercept) # Basal ggtree postestimates_tree <- hmsc_tree %>% force.ultrametric(.,method="extend") %>% ggtree(., size = 0.3) # Phylums phylums <- genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% hmsc_tree$tip.label) %>% arrange(match(genome, hmsc_tree$tip.label)) %>% mutate(phylum = factor(phylum, levels = unique(phylum))) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% select(phylum) #Add phylum colors next to the tree tips postestimates_tree <- gheatmap(postestimates_tree, phylums, offset=-0.2, width=0.1, colnames=FALSE) + scale_fill_manual(values=phylum_colors)+ labs(fill="Phylum") #Reset fill scale to use a different colour profile in the heatmap postestimates_tree <- postestimates_tree + new_scale_fill() # Add posterior significant heatmap postestimates_tree <- gheatmap(postestimates_tree, post_table, offset=0, width=0.5, colnames=TRUE, colnames_position="top",colnames_angle=90, colnames_offset_y=1, hjust=0) + scale_fill_manual(values=c("#be3e2b","#f4f4f4","#b2b530"))+ labs(fill="Trend") postestimates_tree + vexpand(.30, 1) # Adjust p-values using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to identify functional elements that differ significantly between devil-associated groups. functional_differences_devil <- elements_response %>% filter(devil !="Neutral") %>% mutate(devil = droplevels(devil)) %>% group_by(GIFT) %>% summarise( n_pos = sum(devil == "Positive"), n_neg = sum(devil == "Negative"), mean_pos = mean(value[devil == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_neg = mean(value[devil == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE), diff = mean_pos - mean_neg, p = if (n_pos > 1 && n_neg > 1 && stats::sd(value[devil == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0 && stats::sd(value[devil == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0) { stats::t.test(value ~ devil, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value } else NA_real_ , .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")) %>% arrange(p_adj) Note: Create a volcano plot visualizing functional differences between positive and negative devil-associated genomes. Plot mean difference (fold change) against -log10(FDR), with functional elements colored by their functional group. Highlight significant elements that meet both fold change and FDR thresholds, with labels for the most significant hits. fc_threshold <- 0.2 # minimum absolute mean difference to call interesting fdr_threshold <- 0.05 # BH-adjusted p-value cutoff functional_differences_devil_logfold <- functional_differences_devil %>% mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% mutate( # guard against p_adj = 0 or NA p_adj_plot = ifelse(is.na(p_adj) | p_adj == 0, .Machine$double.xmin, p_adj), neglog10_fdr = -log10(p_adj_plot), hit = !is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < fdr_threshold & abs(diff) >= fc_threshold ) %>% mutate(func = ifelse(hit, func, "NS")) %>% filter(neglog10_fdr<20) palette_df <- functional_differences_devil_logfold %>% dplyr::distinct(func) %>% dplyr::left_join( gift_colors %>% dplyr::select(func = Code_function, Color), by = "func" ) %>% dplyr::mutate( Color = dplyr::case_when( func == "NS" & is.na(Color) ~ "grey70", is.na(Color) ~ "#999999", TRUE ~ Color ) ) color_values <- setNames(palette_df$Color, palette_df$func) functional_differences_devil_logfold %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = neglog10_fdr, color=func)) + geom_point(aes(color = func), alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-fc_threshold, fc_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0,15)+ xlim(-0.6,0.6)+ ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = subset(functional_differences_devil_logfold, hit), aes(label = GIFT), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0 ) + scale_color_manual(values = color_values, breaks = names(color_values)) + labs( x = "Mean difference (Positive − Negative)", y = expression(-log[10]("FDR (BH)")), color = "Group", subtitle = paste0("Thresholds: |diff| ≥ ", fc_threshold, ", FDR < ", fdr_threshold) ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) Note: Aggregate devil β coefficients to the functional group level by calculating mean β across all genomes carrying each functional trait. Summarise devil β across genomes for each functional group devil_func_summary <- genome_func %>% dplyr::left_join(devil_ci %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean, q10, q90), by = "genome") %>% dplyr::group_by(func) %>% dplyr::summarise( n_genomes = sum(!is.na(mean)), mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), q90_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) %>% dplyr::filter(n_genomes >= 3) # Take top 15 positive & top 15 negative functions N_top <- 15 devil_func_top <- dplyr::bind_rows( devil_func_summary %>% dplyr::slice_max(order_by = mean_beta, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE), devil_func_summary %>% dplyr::slice_min(order_by = mean_beta, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) ) %>% dplyr::distinct(func, .keep_all = TRUE) # Filter to genomes with credible non-zero effects (where the credible interval does not include zero) and visualize these with error bars, ordered by mean β value. temp_q <- getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_16, parName = "Beta", q = c(0.1, 0.9))$q idx_temp <- which(m$covNames == "temperature") n_genomes <- length(m$spNames) temp_ci <- map_dfr(1:n_genomes, ~ { tibble( genome = m$spNames[.x], q10 = temp_q[1, idx_temp, .x], q90 = temp_q[2, idx_temp, .x] ) }) %>% right_join(temp_estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") temp_ci %>% filter(q10 > 0 | q90 < 0) %>% ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = forcats::fct_reorder(genome, mean), xmin = q10, xmax = q90, colour = phylum)) + geom_point() + geom_errorbar() + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + scale_color_manual(values = phylum_colors) + theme_minimal() + labs(x = "Temperature β coefficient", y = "Genomes") + theme(legend.position = "none") Note: Identify and visualize the top 30 genomes with the strongest positive and top 30 with the strongest negative credible temperature associations. Create a forest plot showing these top genomes with their credible intervals, faceted by association direction (positive/negative), ordered by mean β coefficient and colored by phylum. # --- Temperature credible intervals: top 30 genomes --- # Keep only genomes with credible non-zero temperature effect temp_ci_sig <- temp_ci %>% dplyr::filter(q10 > 0 | q90 < 0) # 4. Take top 30 positive and top 30 negative genomes N_top <- 30 temp_ci_top <- temp_ci_sig %>% dplyr::slice_max(order_by = mean, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) %>% dplyr::bind_rows( temp_ci_sig %>% dplyr::slice_min(order_by = mean, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) ) %>% dplyr::distinct(genome, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% dplyr::mutate( direction = ifelse(mean > 0, "Positive association", "Negative association"), genome = forcats::fct_reorder(genome, mean) ) # 5. Plot credible intervals for these top genomes temp_ci_top %>% ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = mean, y = genome, xmin = q10, xmax = q90, colour = phylum)) + ggplot2::geom_point() + ggplot2::geom_errorbar(width = 0) + ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = phylum_colors) + ggplot2::facet_grid(direction ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + ggplot2::labs( x = "Temperature β coefficient", y = "Top genomes with credible temperature effect" ) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "right") 15.3.1 2) Temperature – phylum-level summary of β Note: Summarize temperature β coefficients at the phylum level by calculating mean β and 80% credible intervals (10th and 90th percentiles) for each phylum. For each functional element, calculate mean abundances in each group, compute differences, and perform t-tests. Adjust p-values using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to identify functional elements that differ significantly between temperature-associated groups. functional_differences_temperature <- elements_response %>% filter(temperature !="Neutral") %>% mutate(temperature = droplevels(temperature)) %>% group_by(GIFT) %>% summarise( n_pos = sum(temperature == "Positive"), n_neg = sum(temperature == "Negative"), mean_pos = mean(value[temperature == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_neg = mean(value[temperature == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE), diff = mean_pos - mean_neg, p = if (n_pos > 1 && n_neg > 1 && stats::sd(value[temperature == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0 && stats::sd(value[temperature == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0) { stats::t.test(value ~ temperature, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value } else NA_real_ , .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")) %>% arrange(p_adj) Note: Create a volcano plot visualizing functional differences between positive and negative temperature-associated genomes. Plot mean difference (fold change) against -log10(FDR), with functional elements colored by their functional group. Highlight significant elements that meet both fold change and FDR thresholds, with labels for the most significant hits. fc_threshold <- 0.2 # minimum absolute mean difference to call interesting fdr_threshold <- 0.05 # BH-adjusted p-value cutoff functional_differences_temperature_logfold <- functional_differences_temperature %>% mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% mutate( # guard against p_adj = 0 or NA p_adj_plot = ifelse(is.na(p_adj) | p_adj == 0, .Machine$double.xmin, p_adj), neglog10_fdr = -log10(p_adj_plot), hit = !is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < fdr_threshold & abs(diff) >= fc_threshold ) %>% mutate(func = ifelse(hit, func, "NS")) %>% # NS = non-significant / background filter(neglog10_fdr < 20) # ---- Build a safe colour vector for all func levels ---- func_levels <- sort(unique(functional_differences_temperature_logfold$func)) palette_df <- tibble::tibble(func = func_levels) %>% dplyr::left_join( gift_colors %>% dplyr::select(func = Code_function, Color), by = "func" ) %>% dplyr::mutate( Color = dplyr::case_when( func == "NS" & is.na(Color) ~ "grey70", # neutral colour for NS is.na(Color) ~ "black", # fallback for any unknown func TRUE ~ Color ) ) color_values <- setNames(palette_df$Color, palette_df$func) functional_differences_temperature_logfold %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = neglog10_fdr, color = func)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-fc_threshold, fc_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0, 15) + xlim(-0.6, 0.6) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = subset(functional_differences_temperature_logfold, hit), aes(label = GIFT), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0 ) + scale_color_manual(values = color_values) + labs( x = "Mean difference (Positive − Negative)", y = expression(-log[10]("FDR (BH)")), color = "Group", subtitle = paste0( "Thresholds: |diff| ≥ ", fc_threshold, ", FDR < ", fdr_threshold ) ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) Note: Aggregate temperature β coefficients to the functional group level by calculating mean β across all genomes carrying each functional trait. Identify the top 15 functional groups with strongest positive and negative associations, then create a forest plot showing functional group-level associations with credible intervals, colored by functional group. # Map genomes to functional groups (GIFT 3-letter codes) genome_func_temp <- elements_response %>% dplyr::filter(value > 0) %>% dplyr::mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% dplyr::distinct(genome, func) # Summarise temperature β across genomes for each functional group temp_func_summary <- genome_func_temp %>% dplyr::left_join(temp_ci %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean, q10, q90), by = "genome") %>% dplyr::group_by(func) %>% dplyr::summarise( n_genomes = sum(!is.na(mean)), mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), q90_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) %>% dplyr::filter(n_genomes >= 3) # Take top 15 positive & top 15 negative functions N_top <- 15 temp_func_top <- dplyr::bind_rows( temp_func_summary %>% dplyr::slice_max(order_by = mean_beta, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE), temp_func_summary %>% dplyr::slice_min(order_by = mean_beta, n = N_top, with_ties = FALSE) ) %>% dplyr::distinct(func, .keep_all = TRUE) # Add nice labels & colours from gift_colors temp_func_top <- temp_func_top %>% dplyr::left_join( gift_colors %>% dplyr::transmute( func = Code_function, func_label = legend, color = Color ), by = "func" ) %>% dplyr::mutate( func_label = ifelse(is.na(func_label), func, func_label) ) func_cols_temp <- setNames(temp_func_top$color, temp_func_top$func_label) # Forest plot: functional groups for temperature ggplot( temp_func_top, aes(x = mean_beta, y = forcats::fct_reorder(func_label, mean_beta), xmin = q10_fun, xmax = q90_fun, colour = func_label) ) + geom_point(size = 2) + geom_errorbar(width = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + scale_color_manual(values = func_cols_temp, guide = "none") + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + labs( x = "Temperature β (mean across genomes carrying the function)", y = "Functional trait (GIFT group)" )

Chapter 16 Hmsc analysis Note: Load all required data objects including genome counts, metadata, GIFT database, and color schemes. Read GIFT color mapping file to create legend labels for functional groups. load("data/data.Rdata") gift_colors <- read_tsv("data/gift_colors.tsv") %>% mutate(legend=str_c(Code_function," - ",Function)) ## Rows: 21 Columns: 3 ## ── Column specification ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ## Delimiter: "\t" ## chr (3): Code_function, Function, Color ## ## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. Note: Set HMSC model parameters for MCMC sampling: number of samples, thinning interval, transient (burn-in) period, and posterior support thresholds for determining significant associations. #Parameters nSamples=250 thin=1000 transient=nSamples * thin support_threshold=0.9 negsupport_threshold=1-support_threshold Note: Load the unfitted HMSC model object and import the fitted model posterior samples from HPC. The fitted model is downloaded from a remote server, then posterior samples are imported and processed according to the specified sampling parameters. #Load unfitted load(file = "hmsc/model_env") #Load fitted (as a temporary file) tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") options(timeout = max(600, getOption("timeout"))) download.file("https://sid.erda.dk/share_redirect/Gh0WbM42c4/Hmsc_model_env.rds", tmp, mode = "wb") importFromHPC = readRDS(tmp)[[1]] unlink(tmp) postList = importFromHPC[1:4] fit_model_17 = importPosteriorFromHPC(m, postList, nSamples, thin, transient) Note: Compute variance partitioning to quantify the proportion of variance explained by each environmental variable and random effect (animal, site) for each genome. Calculate predicted values and evaluate model fit using R², displaying the distribution of R² values across genomes. # Compute variance partitioning varpart=computeVariancePartitioning(fit_model_17) varpart$vals %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column(var="variable") %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(variable=factor(variable)) %>% group_by(variable) %>% summarise(mean=mean(value)*100,sd=sd(value)*100) %>% tt() .table td.tinytable_css_u3cxoam6g0tn76mazi0c, .table th.tinytable_css_u3cxoam6g0tn76mazi0c { border-top: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.05em; } .table td.tinytable_css_rnl3j5xl67t57qqftlch, .table th.tinytable_css_rnl3j5xl67t57qqftlch { border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; } variable mean sd density 4.958057 4.284819 devil 3.724020 3.591131 diversity 2.134729 2.189738 logseqdepth 7.336904 4.525061 precipitation 5.441304 5.040449 Random: animal 55.193679 17.527386 Random: site 18.938665 14.755341 temperature 2.272642 2.584296 preds = computePredictedValues(fit_model_17) MF = evaluateModelFit(hM=fit_model_17, predY=preds) hist(MF$R2, xlim = c(0,1), main=paste0("Mean = ", round(mean(MF$R2),2))) Note: Create a phylogenetic tree visualization with variance partitioning results displayed as stacked bars next to each tip. The tree shows phylum annotations and variance contributions from each predictor variable, allowing visualization of how environmental and random effects vary across the phylogenetic tree. # 1) Build the phylogeny in the same species set/order as varpart vp_tree_phylo <- genome_tree %>% keep.tip(tip = colnames(varpart$vals)) %>% force.ultrametric(method = "extend") vp_tree <- ggtree(vp_tree_phylo, size = 0.3) # 2) Phylum annotation in tree tip order phylums_vp <- genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% vp_tree$data$label) %>% arrange(match(genome, vp_tree$data$label)) %>% mutate(phylum = factor(phylum, levels = unique(phylum))) %>% column_to_rownames("genome") %>% select(phylum) vp_tree <- gheatmap( vp_tree, phylums_vp, offset = -0.2, width = 0.1, colnames = FALSE ) + scale_fill_manual(values = phylum_colors) + labs(fill = "Phylum") # start a new fill scale for the variance bars vp_tree <- vp_tree + new_scale_fill() # 3) Long variance-partitioning table varpart_long <- varpart$vals %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("variable") %>% pivot_longer( cols = -variable, names_to = "label", # must be 'label' to match tree tip labels values_to = "value" ) %>% mutate( # reorder predictors in a sensible way for the legend variable = factor( variable, levels = rev(c( "devil", "temperature", "density", "development", "weight", "precipitation", "diversity", "logseqdepth", "Random: animal", "Random: site" )) ) ) # 4) Add stacked bars with geom_fruit vp_tree + geom_fruit( data = varpart_long, geom = geom_bar, mapping = aes( x = value, y = label, fill = variable ), stat = "identity", orientation = "y", pwidth = 2, offset = 0.05 ) + labs(fill = "Variable") 16.1 Phylogenetic signal Note: Assess phylogenetic signal in the model by extracting the Rho parameter from the posterior distribution. Rho quantifies the strength of phylogenetic correlation in species responses, with values near 1 indicating strong phylogenetic signal and values near 0 indicating weak signal. Calculate credible intervals and visualize the posterior distribution. # Convert to coda object to inspect Rho (phylogenetic signal) mpost <- convertToCodaObject(fit_model_17) # Overall Rho posterior (phylogenetic signal on the species random effect) rho_vec <- unlist(mpost$Rho) # 90% credible interval and median rho_summary <- quantile(rho_vec, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) rho_summary # Optional: density plot for the appendix plot(density(rho_vec), main = "Posterior of phylogenetic signal (Rho)", xlab = "Rho") abline(v = rho_summary[2], col = "red", lty = 2) 16.2 Create posterior estimates table Note: Extract posterior support values and create a table for downstream analysis. This is separated from the visualization chunk to allow execution even when ggtree plots are disabled. hmsc_tree <- genome_tree %>% keep.tip(., tip=m$spNames) # Posterior estimates post_estimates <- getPostEstimate(hM=fit_model_17, parName="Beta")$support %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable=m$covNames) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(trend = case_when( value >= support_threshold ~ "Positive", value <= negsupport_threshold ~ "Negative", TRUE ~ "Neutral")) post_table <- post_estimates %>% mutate(genome=factor(genome, levels=rev(hmsc_tree$tip.label))) %>% select(-trend) %>% mutate(value = case_when( value >= support_threshold ~ "Positive", value <= negsupport_threshold ~ "Negative", TRUE ~ "Neutral")) %>% mutate(value=factor(value, levels=c("Positive","Neutral","Negative"))) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value) %>% rename(intercept=2) %>% column_to_rownames(var="genome") %>% select(-intercept) 16.3 Posterior estimates visualization Note: Visualize posterior support values on a phylogenetic tree. This chunk is set to eval = FALSE due to ggtree compatibility issues. # Basal ggtree postestimates_tree <- hmsc_tree %>% force.ultrametric(.,method="extend") %>% ggtree(., size = 0.3) # Phylums phylums <- genome_metadata %>% filter(genome %in% hmsc_tree$tip.label) %>% arrange(match(genome, hmsc_tree$tip.label)) %>% mutate(phylum = factor(phylum, levels = unique(phylum))) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% select(phylum) #Add phylum colors next to the tree tips postestimates_tree <- gheatmap(postestimates_tree, phylums, offset=-0.2, width=0.1, colnames=FALSE) + scale_fill_manual(values=phylum_colors)+ labs(fill="Phylum") #Reset fill scale to use a different colour profile in the heatmap postestimates_tree <- postestimates_tree + new_scale_fill() # Add posterior significant heatmap postestimates_tree <- gheatmap(postestimates_tree, post_table, offset=0, width=0.5, colnames=TRUE, colnames_position="top",colnames_angle=90, colnames_offset_y=1, hjust=0) + scale_fill_manual(values=c("#be3e2b","#f4f4f4","#b2b530"))+ labs(fill="Trend") postestimates_tree + vexpand(.30, 1) # expand top Note: Examine the congruence between devil and temperature associations at the taxonomic level. Create contingency tables showing how many genomes have each combination of devil and temperature responses (positive, negative, neutral). Visualize taxonomic patterns by phylum to identify whether certain taxonomic groups show consistent response patterns. # Long table of trends for devil and temperature per genome devil_temp_trends <- post_table %>% rownames_to_column("genome") %>% select(genome, devil, temperature) %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") # Overall contingency of trends devil_temp_tab <- devil_temp_trends %>% count(devil, temperature) %>% arrange(desc(n)) devil_temp_tab %>% tt() .table td.tinytable_css_uv2unltusa8xn0rz3ypt, .table th.tinytable_css_uv2unltusa8xn0rz3ypt { border-top: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.05em; } .table td.tinytable_css_jlp7n1iaxrjvn340c0az, .table th.tinytable_css_jlp7n1iaxrjvn340c0az { border-bottom: solid #d3d8dc 0.1em; } devil temperature n Positive Neutral 258 Positive Positive 104 Neutral Neutral 98 Positive Negative 44 Negative Neutral 26 Neutral Negative 24 Negative Positive 9 Neutral Positive 8 Negative Negative 5 # Phylum-level congruence: how many genomes in each combo devil_temp_phylum <- devil_temp_trends %>% group_by(phylum, devil, temperature) %>% summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") # Keep only non-zero combos (for cleaner plots) devil_temp_phylum %>% filter(n > 0) %>% ggplot(aes(x = devil, y = temperature, fill = n)) + geom_tile() + facet_wrap(~ phylum) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightgrey", high = "blue") + labs( x = "Devil association", y = "Temperature association", fill = "Number of genomes", title = "Taxonomic congruence of devil vs temperature responses" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 8) Note: Map GIFT functional annotations (bundle-level) to element-level for genomes included in the HMSC model. Filter to genomes with non-neutral responses for both variables, then summarize functional element signals by devil-temperature response combinations. Aggregate to functional groups and visualize the top 12 most variable functional groups to identify functional traits that show different patterns across response combinations. # elements_response has: genome, GIFT, value, and trend columns (devil, temperature, ...) # Focus on non-neutral responses for both variables elem_dev_temp <- elements_response %>% filter(devil != "Neutral", temperature != "Neutral") %>% mutate( devil = droplevels(devil), temperature = droplevels(temperature) ) # Summarise at the element level: mean value per devil/temperature combo func_congruence_elem <- elem_dev_temp %>% group_by(GIFT, devil, temperature) %>% summarise( mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), n = n(), .groups = "drop" ) # Collapse to functional group (Code_function) func_congruence_group <- func_congruence_elem %>% left_join(GIFT_db, by = c("GIFT" = "Code_bundle")) %>% group_by(Code_function, devil, temperature) %>% summarise( mean_val = mean(mean_val, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) # For readability, keep only functional groups that show some variation interesting_funcs <- func_congruence_group %>% group_by(Code_function) %>% summarise(range_val = max(mean_val) - min(mean_val), .groups = "drop") %>% slice_max(order_by = range_val, n = 12) %>% pull(Code_function) func_congruence_group %>% filter(Code_function %in% interesting_funcs) %>% ggplot(aes(x = devil, y = temperature, fill = mean_val)) + geom_tile() + facet_wrap(~ Code_function) + scale_fill_gradient2() + labs( x = "Devil association", y = "Temperature association", fill = "Mean element signal", title = "Functional congruence of devil vs temperature responses" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 8) 16.4 Association with devil Note: Summarize devil associations across taxonomic levels. Adjust p-values using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to identify functional elements that differ significantly between devil-associated groups. functional_differences_devil <- elements_response %>% filter(devil !="Neutral") %>% mutate(devil = droplevels(devil)) %>% group_by(GIFT) %>% summarise( n_pos = sum(devil == "Positive"), n_neg = sum(devil == "Negative"), mean_pos = mean(value[devil == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_neg = mean(value[devil == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE), diff = mean_pos - mean_neg, p = if (n_pos > 1 && n_neg > 1 && stats::sd(value[devil == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0 && stats::sd(value[devil == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0) { stats::t.test(value ~ devil, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value } else NA_real_ , .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")) %>% arrange(p_adj) Note: Create a volcano plot visualizing functional differences between positive and negative devil-associated genomes. Plot mean difference (fold change) against -log10(FDR), with functional elements colored by their functional group. Highlight significant elements that meet both fold change and FDR thresholds, with labels for the most significant hits. fc_threshold <- 0.2 # minimum absolute mean difference to call interesting fdr_threshold <- 0.05 # BH-adjusted p-value cutoff functional_differences_devil_logfold <- functional_differences_devil %>% mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% mutate( # guard against p_adj = 0 or NA p_adj_plot = ifelse(is.na(p_adj) | p_adj == 0, .Machine$double.xmin, p_adj), neglog10_fdr = -log10(p_adj_plot), hit = !is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < fdr_threshold & abs(diff) >= fc_threshold ) %>% mutate(func = ifelse(hit, func, "NS")) %>% filter(neglog10_fdr<20) palette_df <- functional_differences_devil_logfold %>% dplyr::distinct(func) %>% dplyr::left_join( gift_colors %>% dplyr::select(func = Code_function, Color), by = "func" ) %>% dplyr::mutate( Color = dplyr::case_when( func == "NS" & is.na(Color) ~ "grey70", is.na(Color) ~ "#999999", TRUE ~ Color ) ) color_values <- setNames(palette_df$Color, palette_df$func) functional_differences_devil_logfold %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = neglog10_fdr, color=func)) + geom_point(aes(color = func), alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-fc_threshold, fc_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0,15)+ xlim(-0.6,0.6)+ ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = subset(functional_differences_devil_logfold, hit), aes(label = GIFT), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0 ) + scale_color_manual(values = color_values, breaks = names(color_values)) + labs( x = "Mean difference (Positive − Negative)", y = expression(-log[10]("FDR (BH)")), color = "Group", subtitle = paste0("Thresholds: |diff| ≥ ", fc_threshold, ", FDR < ", fdr_threshold) ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) Note: Aggregate devil β coefficients to the functional group level by calculating mean β across all genomes carrying each functional trait. Map genomes to functional groups (GIFT 3-letter "func" code) genome_func <- elements_response %>% dplyr::filter(value > 0) %>% dplyr::mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% dplyr::distinct(genome, func) # Summarise devil β across genomes for each functional group devil_func_summary <- genome_func %>% dplyr::left_join(devil_ci %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean, q10, q90), by = "genome") %>% dplyr::group_by(func) %>% dplyr::summarise( n_genomes = sum(!is.na(mean)), mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), q90_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) %>% dplyr::filter(n_genomes >= 3) #
